name: Storage partitioning
plain: Browsers key embedded storage by the top site so a tracker sees a separate store on each site.
meaning: Cuts the main cross-site tracking path: a widget on site A and site B no longer shares one cookie or localStorage. Embeds can still track within one site, and workarounds shift to link decoration, redirects and server side IDs.

web.api: Browser behaviour keyed by (top-level site, frame site); use Storage Access API to opt out

access.revocation: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

limits.headline: Can't use the same embedded storage to recognize you across different sites
limits.user_action: Nothing. Your browser does it for you whenever a page is embedded.
can: Store data separately for each site that embeds it
Still remember you on one site
Ask for its own cookies back, if you allow
cannot: Share one stored copy across the sites that embed it
Link a visit on one site to a visit on another through that storage
Skip the Storage Access prompt where browsers require it

story.what_it_is: Browsers give an embedded site a separate store on every site that embeds it, so trackers cannot link you.

marketing.name: State partitioning
marketing.pitch: Mozilla explains how Firefox splits stored data by the top site to stop cross site tracking.

marketing.name: Tracking Prevention
marketing.pitch: Apple describes how Safari limits cross site tracking, including how embedded storage is isolated.

story.for_you: You get this for free. A tracker or like button embedded on two sites can no longer recognise you as the same person using its own stored data.
story.for_makers: It is a big win for privacy and a loss for old style cross site tracking. Ad firms must move to other signals. Honest embeds, like logins and chat, may need to ask for access.

use_cases.example: An ad network embedded on two news sites sees two different, unlinked visitors instead of one person.
A like or share button on a blog can no longer use its own cookie to see which other sites you visit.
An embedded video player forgets your login on each site until it asks for access.
A support chat widget on a company site keeps a chat only for that site, not across the web.
A game portal that embeds each game keeps game saves apart per portal.
A measurement firm can no longer follow a visitor across client sites using embedded storage.
A fraud service embedded on many sites loses a shared ID and must use other signals.

technical_bounds: Third party frames get a different store on each top site
Includes cookies (Firefox, Safari), localStorage, IndexedDB, Cache, BroadcastChannel, SharedWorker
Chrome partitions storage but keeps unpartitioned cookies as a user choice

history.change: Full third party cookie blocking and partitioned storage in ITP
Total Cookie Protection by default for all users
Third party storage partitioning rollout for storage and communication APIs
